Explore Outdoors: The Geminid meteor shower peaks in December

Grab the blankets and some hot cocoa. In this week's Explore Outdoors, we're going stargazing

SACRAMENTO, Calif. —

One of the best meteor showers is about to begin: The Geminid Meteor Shower. It happens every year during the month of December, typically peaking on the 13th and 14th, with up to 10 meteors streaking through the night sky each hour

Unlike typical meteor showers that occur as the Earth passes through the debris cloud of a comet, these meteors are debris left behind from a large asteroid whose orbit passes close to the sun.

"The surface, we think, is like getting baked by the sun and basically just flaking off, and that is leaving behind these chunks of material that are often denser and made from different materials than cometary particles are. So one of the other things that tends to be exciting about the Geminid meteor shower is you can see different colors," says Kyle Watters, planetarium coordinator at California State University Sacramento.

Look toward the Gemini constellation and the easiest way to find it is to locate one of the most recognizable constellations in the night sky: Orion, the hunter.

"If you draw an imaginary line going from Orion’s foot up through the belt, through that bright shoulder, and then keep going another body length of Orion, you’ll get to 2 bright stars ... that’s Castor and Pollux, the heads of Gemini, the Twins," says Watters.

The Geminid meteor shower will be visible throughout the night, in the evening. If you can stay up extra late, the best time for viewing is 1 a.m. when Gemini is directly overhead.

While some meteors may be visible in urban areas, for the best viewing you'll want to get away from the lights of the city. Click here for the best dark sky viewing areas.
